entries.title: Unit Bias – when one unit quietly becomes the ‘right’ amount
entries.description:
Unit bias is our tendency to treat one available unit as a natural or appropriate amount to consume or use. The unit may be a serving, a package, a spoonful, one task, one episode, or another convenient chunk. When the unit becomes larger, we may take more without ever making a clear decision that we need more. Conveniently, the container has offered to think for us.

Where can it show up?
- Food and portions – a larger serving, package, bowl, or scoop can become the default amount.
- Digital products – one playlist, one queue, or one recommended set can define how much feels normal to finish.
- Work – a batch size or ticket bundle can quietly become the amount we believe should be completed in one go.

A better check
- Decide the amount before looking at the default unit when possible.
- Change the unit size and ask whether your preferred total changes with it.
- Separate ‘one unit’ from ‘the amount I actually want or need.’
- Do not assume every portion-size effect is unit bias. Convenience, price, hunger, social norms, waste avoidance, and simple availability can also change behaviour.

The useful lesson is not that units are bad. We need units to organize the world. The problem starts when a packaging decision quietly becomes a personal optimum.

entries.title: Distinction Bias – when comparison makes small differences look important
entries.description:
Distinction bias is our tendency to overpredict how much some differences between options will matter when we compare the options side by side. During comparison, tiny gaps are easy to see. During real experience, when we usually live with one option at a time, many of those gaps become much less important. We can become excellent detectives of differences that our future self may barely notice.

Where can it show up?
- Job offers – a visible salary or benefit difference can dominate factors that shape daily experience.
- Technology – two devices look dramatically different on a specification table, while both may feel almost identical in ordinary use.
- Purchases – comparison pages make measurable differences easy to inspect, even when they have weak practical value.
- Hiring and evaluation – side-by-side scoring can magnify small attribute gaps that matter less in actual performance.

A better check
- Ask how each option would feel if you saw it alone.
- Translate specifications into real use: what changes on a normal Tuesday?
- Separate easy-to-compare attributes from important-but-hard-to-compare attributes.
- Revisit the decision after removing the comparison table.

The evidence is not perfectly tidy. A later close replication found mixed support across two experiments, which is useful information rather than an inconvenience to hide. Distinction bias is a lens with conditions, not a magic stamp for every side-by-side choice.

entries.title: Restraint Bias – when calm us overestimates future self-control
entries.description:
Restraint bias is our tendency to overestimate how well we can control impulses, especially when the temptation or visceral state is not active yet. Calm, rested, full us is often very confident about what hungry, tired, angry, excited, or craving us will do. Future us was apparently not invited to the planning meeting.

Where can it show up?
- Food – we keep tempting food close because we expect willpower to handle it later.
- Smoking or other habits – confidence in self-control can increase exposure to situations that make relapse more likely.
- Spending – we browse a sale ‘just to look’ and assume the decision will remain equally easy after desire is activated.
- Focus – we keep notifications, feeds, or games one tap away because we expect ourselves to ignore them at the exact moment they are designed to be hard to ignore.

A better check
- Design the environment for the state in which self-control will be hardest, not easiest.
- Add friction before temptation becomes active.
- Use past behaviour under similar conditions instead of confidence alone.
- Distinguish confidence from capacity: feeling disciplined now is not a measurement of what you will do later.

This effect does not mean we have no self-control. It means self-control estimates can be state-dependent, and overconfidence can itself change how much temptation we choose to face.

entries.title: Denomination Effect – when the shape of money changes our willingness to spend it
entries.description:
The denomination effect is a tendency to spend equivalent amounts differently depending on how the money is divided. A single large note can feel harder to break than several smaller notes with the same total value. The arithmetic is identical; our spending behaviour has not signed that agreement.

Where can it show up?
- Cash spending – we may protect one larger note while smaller notes or coins disappear more easily.
- Budgeting – separating money into psychologically meaningful units can change how available it feels for spending.
- Travel and foreign currency – unfamiliar denominations can make value harder to feel intuitively.
- Product design and payments – the way a balance is represented may influence whether it feels like one protected amount or many spendable pieces.

A better check
- Convert every option to the same total before deciding.
- Ask whether you would make the same purchase if the same money were represented in different denominations.
- Track the total spent, not just the number or physical size of units left.
- Remember that context matters. Later work shows that denomination effects can interact with memory, monitoring, payment context, and even reverse in situations such as tipping.

Money is fungible in the spreadsheet. In our heads, it often arrives with packaging, labels, friction, and a small amount of theatre.
